newsitem.title: DENMARK: No progress on EU gas directive under Neds - Denma.
newsitem.headline: No progress on EU gas directive under Neds - Denma.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, 10 June, Reuter - The European Union will make no further progress towards concluding a gas directive during the Netherlands' Presidency, Denmark's environment and energy minister Svend Auken told a press conference here on Tuesday.
"There will be no new meeting before the end of the Dutch Presidency," Auken said.
He added that because of recent elections in Britain, France and Ireland, the Dutch Presidency had decided not to pursue the directive.
Auken said the directive was still held up over four main issues, but that a consensus was gradually emerging.
Principally at issue was the extent to which markets should open up.
"The compromise proposals for market opening would allow around 30 percent of the markets to be opened, giving all countries the same minimum opening," he said.
But he added that in Britain, which is fully deregulating, this is considered extremely low, while "others think this is much too high."
"I think 30 percent is the most realistic target," he said. "As a first step it's not that bad a result, but it's no secret that we could also accept a higher market opening."

The other issues to be resolved were whether to allow emerging markets such as Spain, Portugal and Ireland special treatment; third party access to existing pipeline infrastructure; and long term take-or-pay contracts.
On third party access, Auken said the principle has already been established with regard to onshore pipelines, but not with offshore lines.
"The Danish government thinks you can't talk of competition in gas without third party access on and offshore," he said. "This has led to some interesting discussions with our Norwegian brothers."
But Auken believed even though a gas directive is likely to be approved soon, it still would not tackle the two biggest issues, namely security of supply and environmental concerns.
"The environment has not been given enough emphasis," he said, adding that a projection by the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned of the danger of a 50 percent rise in CO2 emissions by 2010.
At least 75 percent of emissions come from only 25 percent of countries in the industrialised world, he said, making it vital that these countries cut emissions.
"Unless we do it in our part of the world, we can't expect emerging markets to do it," he said.
